title: Berkshire Hathaway's Annual Shareholders Meeting, 2018 [Video]
text:
Stay with Yahoo Finance for comprehensive coverage of Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK-A, BRK-B ) is holding its annual shareholder meeting in Omaha, Nebraska. Led by chairman and CEO Warren Buffett and vice chairman Charlie Munger, the meeting has drawn investors, both young and old, seeking wisdom from the investing legends.
The event kicks off at 10:15 a.m. ET, and we’ll have the stream live above.
This year, Berkshire expects to draw a live audience of about 42,000 who’ll be listening for anything that might help them live a more lucrative and fruitful life.
What we’ll be listening for First and foremost, the investing world will want to know his up-to-minute views on the economy and financial markets. While he’s known to consistently reiterate optimism in the long-run, he’ll be expected to address the recent angst. The U.S. economy, which has been in expansion for nine years, appears to be seeing job growth slowing down . Stocks, which have been in a bull market for nine years, touched a high in December and has since been slammed with volatility .
Speaking of stocks, Buffett disclosed on Friday that Berkshire loaded up on shares of Apple ( AAPL ), a tech giant that hit all-time highs on the news.
The audience will surely be interested to hear his latest thoughts on President Trump and the administration’s policies. In his annual letter to shareholders in February, Buffett disclosed that Berkshire Hathaway earned $29 billion in 2017 thanks to tax reform.
Of particular interest will be any new comments he makes about trade policy, which has been dominating the headlines in recent weeks and months. Team Trump has traveled to China in an effort to negotiate trade terms that would be more favorable to the U.S. Trump’s primary negotiating tactic has been the threat of tariffs, which most economists agree is a lose-lose option.
Buffett acknowledges that free trade and globalization, while beneficial, has come with costs . He stressed that America’s leaders need to get better at communicating the benefits of trade.
“You really need an Educator-in-Chief, as president,” Buffett said to Yahoo Finance’s Andy Serwer in March. “That’s what [Franklin Delano] Roosevelt was so good at. We needed an Educator-in-Chief in 1933. And that, you could argue, was the most important part of his presidency.”
This post will be updated throughout the meeting…
(Illustration | David Foster) More It all began with a ‘monumentally stupid decision’ Buffett, 87, first invested in a Berkshire Hathaway, a failing textile company, back in December 1962 accumulating 7% of the company at $7.50 per share. The company was owned by a man named Seabury Stanton, who in 1964 asked Buffett for the price he’d be willing to sell his stake. Buffett said $11.50, and they had a deal.
However, Stanton later turned around and made a tender offer to shareholders for $11.275 per share. Buffett didn’t care for that behavior, so he ended up hanging on.
“That was a monumentally stupid decision,” Buffett said in his 2014 letter to shareholders . “Irritated by Stanton’s chiseling, I ignored his offer and began to aggressively buy more Berkshire shares.”
Buffett took control of the company in May of 1965. And that was followed by another two decades of tough lessons.
“During the 18 years following 1966, we struggled unremittingly with the textile business, all to no avail,” he said. “But stubbornness – stupidity? – has its limits. In 1985, I finally threw in the towel and closed the operation.”
Despite his legend, Buffett’s career is riddled with failures. Ultimately, his real triumph is learning from his mistakes to eventually seal his legacy as the world’s greatest investor.
Furthermore, through letters, interviews, meetings and TV appearances, Buffett has shared his lessons with the public so that they can be better investors themselves. So while many know him as a great investor, there are plenty who will also remember him as a great teacher .
